definition: A cognitive computer is a computer that hardwires artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms into an integrated circuit that closely reproduces the behavior of the human brain.
details: It generally adopts a neuromorphic engineering approach. Synonyms include neuromorphic chip and cognitive chip. In 2023, IBM's proof-of-concept NorthPole chip (optimized for 2-, 4- and 8-bit precision) achieved remarkable performance in image recognition. In 2013, IBM developed Watson, a cognitive computer that uses neural networks and deep learning techniques. The following year, it developed the 2014 TrueNorth microchip architecture which is designed to be closer in structure to the human brain than the von Neumann architecture used in conventional computers. In 2017, Intel also announced its version of a cognitive chip in "Loihi, which it intended to be available to university and research labs in 2018. Intel (most notably with its Pohoiki Beach and Springs systems), Qualcomm, and others are improving neuromorphic processors steadily.

explainer.lead: A cognitive computer builds AI and machine-learning behavior into its circuitry, usually through a brain-inspired neuromorphic design. The aim is hardware whose structure is closer to the human brain than that of a conventional computer, not a machine with human understanding.

tiers.eli5: A cognitive computer puts some brain-inspired learning machinery directly into its chip. It is a bit like building a calculator with parts specially shaped for a particular kind of puzzle, instead of using the same basic parts for every puzzle. That can help with tasks such as recognizing objects in pictures, but it does not mean the machine thinks like a person.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply this approach to neural-network workloads, with IBM's NorthPole demonstrating image recognition at 2-, 4-, and 8-bit precision. Relevant systems include IBM TrueNorth and Intel Loihi, Pohoiki Beach, and Pohoiki Springs; precision support and research-platform availability need checking rather than assuming drop-in use. A cognitive chip is not automatically a general-purpose replacement for a conventional computer.
tiers.paperLevel: A cognitive computer hardwires AI and machine-learning algorithms into an integrated circuit, generally using neuromorphic engineering to reproduce aspects of human-brain behavior rather than merely running AI software on a conventional processor. Named examples include IBM Watson (2013), TrueNorth (2014), and NorthPole (2023), plus Intel Loihi (2017). NorthPole remains a proof of concept, and image-recognition results do not establish general human-like cognition.

explainer.example: A photograph is passed to IBM's 2023 NorthPole proof-of-concept chip for image recognition. The chip performs the computation using 2-, 4-, or 8-bit precision and produces a recognition result; IBM reported remarkable performance.

usedIn.detail: A 2023 proof-of-concept chip optimized for 2-, 4-, and 8-bit precision, demonstrated in image recognition.

usedIn.detail: Loihi was announced in 2017, with Pohoiki Beach and Springs among Intel's neuromorphic research systems.

explainer.intuition: Instead of treating intelligence only as software instructions, build some of the needed computation into the chip itself. Neuromorphic engineering supplies the brain-inspired structural approach.
howItWorks: Choose an AI or machine-learning computation to support in hardware.
Implement its algorithms directly in an integrated circuit.
Organize the circuit using a neuromorphic, brain-inspired approach.
Feed data through the chip to produce results such as image classifications.
explainer.whyItMatters: It connects machine-learning algorithms with the physical design of computing hardware, offering an alternative to conventional von Neumann organization. Systems such as TrueNorth, Loihi, and NorthPole show how this approach has developed across research chips and recognition tasks.
misconceptions: It is not a claim of human consciousness or understanding.
It is not simply AI software running on an ordinary computer; the algorithms are hardwired into circuitry.
Watson and TrueNorth are not interchangeable: one is a cognitive computer system, the other a microchip architecture.
